clinicalPearls: Well-demarcated, uniformly pigmented light- to dark-brown macule or patch, usually present from birth or early childhood
One or a few lesions are common in the general population and usually of no significance
Six or more macules exceeding 5 mm before puberty, or 15 mm after puberty, is a diagnostic criterion for neurofibromatosis type 1
Smooth ('coast of California') borders are typical of neurofibromatosis type 1, whereas irregular ('coast of Maine') borders suggest McCune-Albright syndrome
Axillary or inguinal freckling (Crowe sign) alongside multiple macules further supports neurofibromatosis type 1
The pigment is epidermal and is accentuated on Wood-lamp examination
Assessment should include counting and measuring lesions and screening for other features of neurocutaneous syndromes
reference.pathophysiology: Café-au-lait macules result from increased melanin within basal keratinocytes and melanocytes, often with giant melanosomes (macromelanosomes) on microscopy, while melanocyte numbers remain broadly normal. In neurofibromatosis type 1, loss of neurofibromin dysregulates the RAS signalling pathway and enhances melanocyte activity, accounting for the multiple macules. In McCune-Albright syndrome an activating GNAS mutation similarly increases melanogenesis, producing larger lesions with irregular borders.
additionalInvestigations: Wood-lamp examination to confirm epidermal pigment
Full skin examination for freckling and neurofibromas
Counting and measuring the macules against diagnostic thresholds
Ophthalmology assessment for Lisch nodules and genetics referral where a syndrome is suspected
Family history and review for features of McCune-Albright syndrome
redFlags: Six or more macules with additional features of neurofibromatosis type 1
Irregular-bordered macules with precocious puberty or bony changes suggesting McCune-Albright syndrome
Associated developmental delay, seizures or other neurological concerns
A pigmented lesion showing atypical change that warrants exclusion of another diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Individual macules are entirely benign and permanent; their clinical importance lies in the possibility of an underlying neurocutaneous or endocrine syndrome when they are multiple or atypical.
pitfalls: Dismissing multiple café-au-lait macules without assessing for neurofibromatosis type 1
Failing to measure and count lesions against the diagnostic criteria
Confusing a café-au-lait macule with a Becker naevus or naevus spilus
Overlooking the irregular borders and endocrine clues of McCune-Albright syndrome
management: Reassure that isolated macules are benign and require no active treatment.
Assess against diagnostic thresholds and examine for additional features to identify neurofibromatosis type 1 or McCune-Albright syndrome.
Refer to clinical genetics and, where neurofibromatosis is suspected, to ophthalmology for Lisch nodule assessment.
Arrange surveillance for evolving neurocutaneous or endocrine syndrome features when lesions are multiple or atypical.
Offer cosmetic pigment laser therapy only where lesions cause distress, counselling on recurrence.
Provide genetic counselling and family assessment when an underlying heritable syndrome is confirmed.
